answer:
RESEARCH DRAFT — FOR REVIEW BY A QUALIFIED ATTORNEY. NOT LEGAL ADVICE.

MEMORANDUM

To: Reviewing attorney
From: Legal researcher
Date of research: text verified against legislation.gov.uk as fetched 22 November 2026
Re: Companies Act 2006, section 378 — small-donations exception: monetary ceiling and measuring period

1. Question
A company secretary is checking the small-donations exception in section 378 of the Companies Act 2006. In the text stated to be up to date through 20 November 2026, what donation ceiling and measuring period does that section state?

2. Short answer
In the version of section 378 of the Companies Act 2006 stated to be up to date with all changes known to be in force on or before 20 November 2026, the small-donations exception states:

(a) Monetary ceiling: £5,000 (five thousand pounds sterling).

(b) Measuring period: a rolling period of 12 months ending with the date on which the donation in question is made (not a financial year, calendar year, or other fixed accounting period).

3. Jurisdiction
The provision is United Kingdom legislation. The section is marked “U.K.” on the official revised text, indicating that it applies throughout the United Kingdom (England and Wales, Scotland, and Northern Ireland). The Companies Act 2006 is a UK Public General Act (2006 c. 46). Commencement of section 378 differed by jurisdiction (in force for certain purposes at 1 October 2007 in England, Wales and Scotland, at 1 November 2007 in Northern Ireland, and wholly in force at 1 October 2008), but the in-force text of the section is the same UK-wide provision. No separate England-and-Wales-only, Scottish, or Northern-Ireland-only variant of the ceiling or period appears on the face of the official text.

4. Primary source and version
Act: Companies Act 2006, 2006 c. 46, Part 14 (Control of political donations and expenditure), Exemptions, section 378.

Official source: legislation.gov.uk, Latest available (Revised) text of section 378, https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/section/378, as fetched 22 November 2026 (sha256 2ca6282f9220).

Version statement matching the requested cut-off: the Table of Contents for the Act states: “Companies Act 2006 is up to date with all changes known to be in force on or before 20 November 2026.” (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/contents, fetched 2026-11-22, sha256 8c853c569d95).

The section page banner reads “on or before 22 November 2026.” That is a two-day difference in the editorial “known to be in force” date on the section view versus the Act contents view. It is not a difference in the text of section 378. Every point-in-time version of section 378 fetched — latest revised; as shown at 26 May 2015; at 6 April 2021; and at 1 April 2025 (Welsh interface) — states the identical ceiling of £5,000 and the identical 12-month period. No amendment in force before 20 November 2026 has altered either figure. The section heading in the as-enacted and all revised versions remains: “Donations not amounting to more than £5,000 in any twelve month period.”

5. Statutory text, quoted in full
Companies Act 2006, section 378:

“378  Donations not amounting to more than £5,000 in any twelve month period. U.K.

(1)  Authorisation under this Part is not needed for a donation except to the extent that the total amount of—

(a)  that donation, and

(b)  other relevant donations made in the period of 12 months ending with the date on which that donation is made,

exceeds £5,000.

(2)  In this section—

“donation” means a donation to a political party or other political organisation or to an independent election candidate; and

“other relevant donations” means—

(a)  in relation to a donation made by a company that is not a subsidiary, any other donations made by that company or by any of its subsidiaries;

(b)  in relation to a donation made by a company that is a subsidiary, any other donations made by that company, by any holding company of that company or by any other subsidiary of any such holding company.

(3)  If or to the extent that a donation is exempt by virtue of this section from the requirement of authorisation under this Part, it shall be disregarded in determining what donations are authorised by any resolution passed for the purposes of this Part.”

Source for the quotation: legislation.gov.uk, Companies Act 2006, section 378, latest available (Revised) text, https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/section/378, fetched 2026-11-22. The same words appear in the point-in-time views at 6 April 2021 (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/section/378/2021-04-06) and 1 April 2025 (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/cy/ukpga/2006/46/section/378/2025-04-01).

6. How the ceiling and the period operate (from the statutory words only)

Ceiling. The figure is £5,000. It is stated as an absolute monetary amount in section 378(1) itself. It is not prescribed by cross-reference to another instrument, and no order or secondary legislation is cited on the face of the section as varying it.

Measuring period. The period is “the period of 12 months ending with the date on which that donation is made” (section 378(1)(b)). It is a backward-looking rolling twelve-month window measured from the date of each donation, not the company’s financial year and not a calendar year. The section heading uses the same measure: “any twelve month period.”

What is measured. The £5,000 test is applied to the total of (a) the donation being made plus (b) “other relevant donations” in that rolling 12-month period. “Other relevant donations” aggregates donations across the group: for a non-subsidiary, the company’s own other donations and those of its subsidiaries; for a subsidiary, its own other donations and those of its holding company and the holding company’s other subsidiaries (section 378(2)).

Partial exception. Authorisation under Part 14 is not needed “except to the extent that” the aggregated total exceeds £5,000 (section 378(1)). Donations that are exempt by virtue of the section are disregarded when determining what donations are authorised by a resolution under this Part (section 378(3)).

7. Corroboration
The Explanatory Notes to the Companies Act 2006, commenting on the exemptions in Part 14, state that “section 378 restates the exemption in section 347B of the 1985 Act under which authorisation for donations is not required unless the donation or aggregate amount of the donations by the company exceeds £5,000 in a 12 month period. Donations by other group companies (including subsidiaries) must be taken into account in calculating whether the £5,000 threshold has been exceeded.” (Explanatory Notes to Companies Act 2006, commentary on Part 14, https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/notes/division/10, fetched 2026-11-22, sha256 a8b7a2feacc4.) The Notes are official explanatory material, not the enacted text; they agree with the enacted words quoted in paragraph 5.

8. Authority: where it is solid and where it is thin

Solid. The ceiling and the measuring period are on the face of the enacted section, in the official revised text on legislation.gov.uk, unchanged across every version of the section fetched (latest revised; 2015; 2021; 2025). The Act-level version statement matches the requested date of 20 November 2026. The UK extent marker is on the section.

Thin / to note for the file. (i) The section-view banner says “22 November 2026” rather than “20 November 2026”; the text is the same, but if the reviewing attorney wants the banner date to match the instruction exactly, the Act contents page is the page that says 20 November 2026. (ii) legislation.gov.uk’s own legend warns that “Revised legislation carried on this site may not be fully up to date” and that some effects may be listed but not yet applied to the text. No outstanding change to section 378 is indicated on the pages fetched. (iii) No specific company’s donation amounts or financial year were provided, so this result is the statutory ceiling and period only; it is not a compliance opinion on any actual or proposed donation.

9. What this answer is not
This memorandum locates and quotes the statutory ceiling and measuring period. It does not advise whether any particular donation by any particular company falls within the exception. Applying section 378 to a real donation would require the donation date, the amount, all “other relevant donations” by the company and its group in the preceding 12 months, and confirmation that the recipient is a political party, other political organisation, or independent election candidate within section 378(2) and the related Part 14 definitions (sections 363–364).

10. Result
Donation ceiling: £5,000.
Measuring period: 12 months, being the period of 12 months ending with the date on which that donation is made.
Jurisdiction: United Kingdom.
Version: Companies Act 2006 s. 378, official revised text stated to be up to date with all changes known to be in force on or before 20 November 2026 (Act contents page); text identical in all retrieved versions.

Draft for attorney review. Not legal advice.

MEMORANDUM

To: Reviewing attorney
From: Legal researcher
Date of research: 22 November 2026
Re: Companies Act 2006 s.586 — minimum paid-up fraction before a public company may allot shares
Jurisdiction: United Kingdom (England and Wales, Scotland, and Northern Ireland). The Companies Act 2006 is a UK Public General Act (2006 c. 46). A rule stated here is not assumed to hold outside that jurisdiction.

QUESTION

Before a public company allots shares, what minimum paid-up fraction is stated by section 586 of the Companies Act 2006, using the text stated to be up to date through 20 November 2026?

ANSWER

One-quarter (1/4) of the share's nominal value, together with the whole of any premium on the share.

AUTHORITY (PRIMARY SOURCE, CITED IN FULL)

Companies Act 2006, section 586 (Public companies: shares must be at least one-quarter paid up), as revised at https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/section/586 (fetched 22 November 2026). The page states: "Companies Act 2006, Section 586 is up to date with all changes known to be in force on or before 21 November 2026." That revised text therefore covers the requested currency of 20 November 2026. The operative words are the same in the 1 October 2009 version and the 26 June 2017 point-in-time version of the same section, so the fraction has not been amended.

STATUTORY TEXT

Section 586 provides:

"(1) A public company must not allot a share except as paid up at least as to one-quarter of its nominal value and the whole of any premium on it.
(2) This does not apply to shares allotted in pursuance of an employees' share scheme.
(3) If a company allots a share in contravention of this section—
(a) the share is to be treated as if one-quarter of its nominal value, together with the whole of any premium on it, had been received, and
(b) the allottee is liable to pay the company the minimum amount which should have been received in respect of the share under subsection (1) (less the value of any consideration actually applied in payment up, to any extent, of the share and any premium on it), with interest at the appropriate rate.
(4) Subsection (3) does not apply to the allotment of bonus shares, unless the allottee knew or ought to have known the shares were allotted in contravention of this section."

Source: legislation.gov.uk, Companies Act 2006 c. 46, s. 586, latest revised text, fetched 22 November 2026.

APPLICATION

The minimum paid-up fraction stated by section 586(1) is one-quarter of nominal value. That fraction is measured against the share's nominal value, not its market value. In addition to that one-quarter, the whole of any premium on the share must also be paid up. Both requirements apply at the time of allotment by a public company.

Two limits on the rule, taken from the same section, should be noted for the reviewing attorney:

1. Employees' share schemes. Section 586(2) disapplies the section from shares allotted in pursuance of an employees' share scheme.

2. Consequences of contravention. Under section 586(3), a non-compliant allotment is treated as if the one-quarter of nominal value plus the whole premium had been received, and the allottee is liable to pay the shortfall (with interest at the appropriate rate). Under section 586(4), that consequence does not apply to bonus shares unless the allottee knew or ought to have known of the contravention.

The chapter heading in the Act (Part 17, Chapter 5, "Additional rules for public companies") and the section heading ("Public companies: shares must be at least one-quarter paid up") confirm that the rule is specific to public companies. Related provisions in the same chapter (sections 584, 585, 587–592) address other public-company payment rules and are not needed to answer the fraction question.

CURRENCY CHECK

The constraint was to use the text up to date through 20 November 2026. The version consulted is the legislation.gov.uk revised text stated to include all changes in force on or before 21 November 2026. No amendment to the operative language of section 586(1) appears in that version, in the 2017-06-26 point-in-time version (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/section/586/2017-06-26), or in the 2009-10-01 version. The answer is therefore the same on the requested date.

WHERE AUTHORITY IS THIN OR ASSUMPTIONS ARE MADE

The fraction itself is stated on the face of the statute and is not thin. The following points are not established by the materials fetched and are flagged rather than filled in:

- The request does not identify a particular company or transaction. The answer assumes the company is a public company to which the Companies Act 2006 applies (a company registered under the Companies Acts in the United Kingdom). Overseas companies and other entities are outside the scope of this answer.
- The request does not state the allotment date. Paid-up value is measured as at allotment. If the allotment is on or before 20 November 2026, the text used above is the correct one.
- Whether the allotment falls within an employees' share scheme (s. 586(2)), or whether non-cash consideration or the independent-valuation regime in Chapter 6 of Part 17 is engaged, depends on facts not supplied.

This memorandum is a draft for review by a qualified attorney. It is not legal advice.

RESULT VALUE

Ask 1 (value): 1/4, unit: of the nominal value of the share. The whole of any premium must also be paid up (same subsection).
Ask 2 is a constraint on the text used, not a value or verdict ask; it is satisfied by the currency check above and has no results entry.

The first reads: "Companies Act 2006, Section 586 is up to date with all changes known to be in force on or before 21 November 2026."

MEMORANDUM

To: Reviewing attorney
From: Legal researcher
Date of snapshot: 2026-11-21 (sources fetched 2026-11-22)
Re: Word limits for motion memoranda in FTC adjudicative proceedings under 16 CFR Part 3

1. Jurisdiction and governing body

United States federal administrative law. The rules that govern are the Federal Trade Commission's Rules of Practice for Adjudicative Proceedings, 16 C.F.R. Part 3. Those rules apply to formal adjudicative proceedings conducted by the Commission under statutes administered by the Commission that require determination on the record after opportunity for an agency hearing. 16 C.F.R. § 3.2 (defining "adjudicative proceedings"); see also 16 C.F.R. § 3.1 (scope of the rules in Part 3).

This is not the federal-court regime (Fed. R. Civ. P. / Fed. R. App. P.) and not an ALJ local-practice overlay. The limits below are the ones written into the Code of Federal Regulations itself.

2. Direct answer — 16 C.F.R. § 3.22(c)

The operative sentence is 16 C.F.R. § 3.22(c) (Content):

    "Memoranda in support of, or in opposition to, any dispositive motion shall not exceed 10,000 words. Memoranda in support of, or in opposition to, any other motion shall not exceed 2,500 words. Any reply in support of a dispositive motion shall not exceed 5,000 words and any reply in support of any other motion authorized by the Administrative Law Judge or the Commission shall not exceed 1,250 words."

Therefore, as in force on 2026-11-21:

- Memorandum supporting or opposing a dispositive motion: 10,000 words.
- Memorandum supporting or opposing any other motion: 2,500 words.

3. Primary sources, cited in full

(a) Codified text in force on the snapshot date:

- 16 C.F.R. § 3.22(c) (2026), Motions — Content. Confirmed in the official 2026 annual edition: Part 3 — Rules of Practice for Adjudicative Proceedings, 16 C.F.R. pt. 3 (2026), available at govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2026-title16-vol1/pdf/CFR-2026-title16-vol1-part3.pdf (fetched 2026-11-22); and in the e-CFR current text of § 3.22 and of Subpart C, ecfr.gov/current/title-16/part-3/section-3.22 and ecfr.gov/current/title-16/chapter-I/subchapter-A/part-3/subpart-C/ (fetched 2026-11-22).

(b) Adopting and amending Federal Register notices (same numeric limits; no later amendment changed them):

- Rules of Practice, 16 C.F.R. Parts 3 and 4, 74 Fed. Reg. 1821 (Jan. 13, 2009) (adopting the 10,000 / 2,500 / 5,000 / 1,250 structure in proposed paragraph (c), described by the Commission as approximately 40 and 10 double-spaced pages respectively).
- 80 Fed. Reg. 15160, 15161 (Mar. 23, 2015) (revising § 3.22; the word-count sentences at issue were not changed in number; the 2015 amendment is the last cited amendment on the e-CFR credit line for § 3.22).

The e-CFR credit line for § 3.22 reads: "[74 FR 1821, Jan. 13, 2009, as amended at 80 FR 15160, Mar. 23, 2015]." No amendment after 2015 is credited on the current text fetched on 2026-11-22. The 2026 annual CFR edition reproduces the same sentences. I therefore treat the 10,000- and 2,500-word limits as the text in force on 2026-11-21.

4. What the word count includes and excludes — § 3.22(c) (continuation) and the parallel form paragraph

The same paragraph continues:

    "These word count limitations include headings, footnotes, and quotations, but do not include the cover, table of contents, table of citations or authorities, glossaries, statements with respect to oral argument, any addendums containing statutes, rules or regulations, any certificates of counsel, proposed form of order, and any attachment required by § 3.45(e)."

The e-CFR current § 3.22 page and the 2026 govinfo PDF state this exclusion list; the e-CFR Subpart C compilation states it in materially identical words. Count headings, footnotes, and quotations. Do not count the cover, tables, glossaries, oral-argument statements, statutory addenda, counsel certificates, the proposed order, or a § 3.45(e) attachment.

5. Adjacent limits that are not the answer to the question asked, but are easy to confuse with it

The reviewing attorney should not conflate the following with § 3.22(c):

- Replies. A reply in support of a dispositive motion is 5,000 words; a reply in support of any other motion authorized by the ALJ or the Commission is 1,250 words. 16 C.F.R. § 3.22(c). The question asked about memoranda in support of or in opposition to motions — i.e., opening and opposition memoranda — not replies.
- Motions following denial of Section 13(b) preliminary injunctive relief. "Memoranda in support of or in opposition to motions authorized by this section shall not exceed 10,000 words," with the same include/exclude list. 16 C.F.R. § 3.26(e) (credit line: 80 Fed. Reg. 15161, Mar. 23, 2015). That 10,000-word figure is a separate rule for a separate motion type; it happens to match the dispositive-motion number.
- Interlocutory applications to the Commission. "Neither the application for review nor the answer shall exceed 2,500 words," with the same include/exclude list. 16 C.F.R. § 3.23 (application for review of an ALJ ruling).
- Commission review of an initial decision (appeal briefs). Opening brief and answering brief: 14,000 words each; reply brief: 7,000 words; all "without leave of the Commission." 16 C.F.R. § 3.51(c) / the review-brief provisions of Subpart C as codified (the e-CFR Part 3 text fetched quotes these figures in the answering/reply-brief paragraphs).
- Extensions of word-count limits are disfavored and "will only be granted where a party can make a strong showing that undue prejudice would result from complying with the existing limit." 16 C.F.R. Part 3 (e-CFR current text, word-count limitations paragraph).

6. What "dispositive motion" means here

Section 3.22(c) uses the phrase "any dispositive motion" without a subsection definition. The Commission's adopting notice, 74 Fed. Reg. 1821 (Jan. 13, 2009), discusses the 10,000-word cap as applying to "dispositive motions" and pairs it with a Commission deadline to resolve "any dispositive motion within 45 days," and the rules separately treat summary decision as a principal dispositive device: 16 C.F.R. § 3.24(a) (summary decision), with memoranda "consistent with § 3.22(c)." In practice the 10,000-word cap is the one that applies to case-dispositive papers (summary decision, and any motion that disposes of the complaint or of claims). Motions that are not dispositive — including discovery motions, extension requests, and other interlocutory motions — take the 2,500-word cap. If a particular motion's classification is contested, the reviewing attorney should treat the safer course as seeking leave, or as using the 10,000-word cap only where the motion would end the proceeding or a claim.

7. Who must apply the limits, and caveats on case-specific overlay

The limits are imposed by the CFR, not by leave of the ALJ. A scheduling order under § 3.21 or a standing order may impose tighter limits; it may not lawfully relax the CFR ceiling without the strong-showing standard quoted above. Nothing in the materials reviewed is an FTC local rule, standing order, or case scheduling order that changes the 10,000 / 2,500 numbers on or before 2026-11-21.

8. Bottom line

As in force on 2026-11-21, in a United States Federal Trade Commission adjudicative proceeding under 16 C.F.R. Part 3:

- Dispositive-motion memoranda (support or opposition): 10,000 words. 16 C.F.R. § 3.22(c).
- Any other motion, memoranda (support or opposition): 2,500 words. 16 C.F.R. § 3.22(c).

This draft is for attorney review. It is not legal advice. The reviewing attorney should confirm against the e-CFR on the filing date that § 3.22 has not been further amended, and should check the assigned ALJ's scheduling and standing orders for any tighter case-specific cap.

The first reads: "Memoranda in support of, or in opposition to, any dispositive motion shall not exceed 10,000 words."

answer:

Jurisdiction: European Union. Primary source: Directive 2011/83/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 25 October 2011 on consumer rights, amending Council Directive 93/13/EEC and Directive 1999/44/EC and repealing Council Directive 85/577/EEC and Directive 97/7/EC, OJ L 304, 22.11.2011, p. 64–88, CELEX 32011L0083 (the “Directive”). This memorandum applies the Directive text only. It is not an opinion on any Member State’s transposition. Article 24 of the Directive required Member States to adopt implementing measures by 13 December 2013; national law may therefore frame, extend or specify details beyond the Directive text and must be checked before the instructions are published.

QUESTION

An online retailer is drafting withdrawal instructions. Using the text at CELEX 32011L0083: when does the 14-day withdrawal period expire (a) for a service contract and (b) for a sales contract?

SHORT ANSWER

Under Article 9(2) of the Directive:

(a) Service contract. The withdrawal period expires after 14 days from the day of the conclusion of the contract. Article 9(2), first indent, CELEX 32011L0083.

(b) Sales contract. The withdrawal period expires after 14 days from the day on which the consumer, or a third party other than the carrier and indicated by the consumer, acquires physical possession of the goods. Article 9(2), second indent, CELEX 32011L0083. Where the order involves multiple goods delivered separately, a good in multiple lots or pieces, or regular delivery over a defined period, the starting day is the day of possession of the last good, the last lot or piece, or the first good, respectively (Article 9(2), second indent, points (i)–(iii)).

In both cases the starting day is the trigger day named in Article 9(2); the period runs for 14 days from that day and expires at the end of the 14th day after it. Example: a service contract concluded on 1 March expires at the end of 15 March; goods acquired on 1 March expire at the end of 15 March.

CONTROLLING TEXT (quoted in full)

Article 9(1)–(2), CELEX 32011L0083:

“1. The Member States shall ensure that the consumer has a period of 14 days to withdraw from a distance contract or an off-premises contract, as referred to in Article 13(1), without giving any reason and without incurring any costs other than those provided for in Article 13(2) and Article 14.

2. Without prejudice to Article 10, the withdrawal period referred to in paragraph 1 of this Article shall expire after 14 days from:
(a) in the case of service contracts, the day of the conclusion of the contract;
(b) in the case of sales contracts, the day on which the consumer or a third party other than the carrier and indicated by the consumer acquires physical possession of the goods or:
(i) in the case of multiple goods ordered by the consumer in one order and delivered separately, the day on which the consumer or a third party other than the carrier and indicated by the consumer acquires physical possession of the last good;
(ii) in the case of delivery of a good consisting of multiple lots or pieces, the day on which the consumer or a third party other than the carrier and indicated by the consumer acquires physical possession of the last lot or piece;
(iii) in the case of contracts for regular delivery of goods during defined period of time, the day on which the consumer or a third party other than the carrier and indicated by the consumer acquires physical possession of the first good;
(c) in the case of contracts for the supply of water, gas or electricity, where they are not put up for sale in a limited volume or set quantity, of district heating or of digital content which is not supplied on a tangible medium, the day of the conclusion of the contract.”

Relevant definitions, Article 2, CELEX 32011L0083 (the wording below is the EUR-Lex / Publications Office text of the Directive as consolidated; the United Kingdom’s retained version at legislation.gov.uk inserts additional price-payment words in points (5) and (6) that do not appear in the CELEX text and are not relied on here):

“‘sales contract’ means any contract under which the trader transfers or undertakes to transfer ownership of goods to the consumer, including any contract having as its object both goods and services;”

“‘service contract’ means any contract other than a sales contract under which the trader supplies or undertakes to supply a service, including a digital service, to the consumer;”

A hybrid contract (goods and services) is a sales contract under the Article 2 definition, so the goods-delivery start in Article 9(2)(b) applies, not the conclusion-day start in Article 9(2)(a).

APPLICATION

Service contracts (ask 2)

The clock starts on the day the contract is concluded and expires after 14 days from that day. Article 9(2), first indent, CELEX 32011L0083. For a distance or off-premises service contract within Chapter II, that is the default expiry, provided the consumer was given the pre-contractual information on the right of withdrawal required by Article 6(1) and, where applicable, Article 7(1).

If the consumer asked the trader to begin performance during the withdrawal period, Article 7(3) requires the trader to confirm that request on a durable medium. That request does not shorten or restart the Article 9(2)(a) period: the period still expires after 14 days from the day of conclusion. The consequences of early performance are financial and exclusion-based, not a different expiry date: Article 16, point (a), CELEX 32011L0083, provides that Member States shall not provide for the right of withdrawal in respect of “service contracts after the service has been fully performed but, if the contract places the consumer under an obligation to pay, only if the performance has begun with the consumer’s prior express consent and acknowledgement that he will lose his right of withdrawal once the contract has been fully performed by the trader.” The Annex I(A) model information on withdrawal likewise states, for services: “If you requested to begin the performance of services … during the withdrawal period, you shall pay us an amount which is in proportion to what has been provided until you have communicated us your withdrawal from this contract, in comparison with the full coverage of the contract.”

Sales contracts (ask 3)

The clock does not start at conclusion. It starts on the day the consumer, or a third party other than the carrier and indicated by the consumer, acquires physical possession of the goods, and expires after 14 days from that day. Article 9(2), second indent, chapeau, CELEX 32011L0083. “Goods” are tangible movable items (Article 2; water, gas and electricity count as goods only where put up for sale in a limited volume or set quantity).

The three refinements in Article 9(2)(b)(i)–(iii) are part of the same indent and are not optional drafting:
• multiple goods in one order, delivered separately: last good;
• one good in multiple lots or pieces: last lot or piece;
• regular delivery of goods during a defined period: first good.

An online retailer drafting instructions should therefore not use a single fixed “14 days from order” or “14 days from dispatch” formulation for goods. The model instructions in Annex I(A) reflect the Directive: “The withdrawal period will expire after 14 days from the day … [from the day of the conclusion of this contract / from the day on which you acquire, or a third party other than the carrier and indicated by you acquires, physical possession of] the goods.”

CAVEATS THAT DO NOT CHANGE THE TWO VALUES ABOVE

1. Information failure. Article 10, CELEX 32011L0083: if the trader has not provided the information on the right of withdrawal required by Article 6(1)(h) or (i), Article 6(1)(k) and Article 7(1), the withdrawal period expires 12 months after the end of the initial Article 9(2) period, or 14 days after the consumer receives that information if it is provided during that 12-month period. The 14-day figures above assume the consumer was duly informed.

2. Article 9(2)(c) look-alikes. Untethered water, gas or electricity, district heating, and digital content not supplied on a tangible medium start on the day of conclusion, not on delivery. They are not “sales contracts” for Article 9(2)(b) unless the utility is in a limited volume or set quantity.

3. Article 16 exemptions. Certain services and goods carry no withdrawal right at all (for example fully performed service contracts meeting Article 16(a); financial-market price fluctuation; made-to-specification or personalised goods; rapidly deteriorating goods; unsealed hygiene goods; inseparably mixed goods). Where an exemption applies, the question “when does the period expire” does not arise because there is no period.

4. Transposition. The Directive is not self-executing in national courts in the same way as a regulation. Before the retailer’s instructions are used in a given market, check that Member State’s implementing law (and any longer national period or additional formality). The CELEX text is the EU-level baseline used for this draft.

DRAFTING CONSEQUENCE FOR THE RETAILER’S INSTRUCTIONS

Use two start-event formulations, not one:
• Services (and untethered digital content / untethered utilities / district heating): expire after 14 days from the day of conclusion.
• Goods: expire after 14 days from the day of physical possession (or last good / last lot / first good, as applicable), identifying the consumer or the consumer’s indicated third party, and excluding the carrier.

All statements of law above are tied to CELEX 32011L0083, Article 9(1)–(2), Article 2, Article 6, Article 7(3), Article 10, Article 16, Annex I, and Article 24, as indicated. This is a draft for review by a qualified attorney and is not legal advice.

question: Y131
answer:
DRAFT FOR QUALIFIED ATTORNEY REVIEW — TRAINING-MODULE EXTRACT — NOT LEGAL ADVICE

Jurisdiction: Council of Europe / High Contracting Parties to the European Convention on Human Rights (Strasbourg system). A rule stated here is a Convention rule; it is not assumed to hold identically in any particular domestic legal order.

1. The presumption, quoted from the official text

In the European Convention on Human Rights, in the text presented as amended through Protocol No. 15 (CETS No. 213), the presumption that applies to everyone charged with a criminal offence is the presumption of innocence, stated in Article 6, paragraph 2, in these exact words:

    "Everyone charged with a criminal offence shall be presumed innocent until proved guilty according to law."

2. Primary-source citation (full)

European Convention on Human Rights, as amended by Protocols Nos. 11, 14 and 15 and supplemented by Protocols Nos. 1, 4, 6, 7, 12, 13 and 16, Article 6, paragraph 2 (Council of Europe, official English text). The Council of Europe publishes this consolidated text on the European Court of Human Rights website at https://www.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/convention_ENG, where the cover note states that "[t]he text of the Convention is presented as amended by the provisions of Protocol No. 15 (CETS No. 213) as from its entry into force on 1 August 2021 and of Protocol No. 14 (CETS No. 194) as from its entry into force on 1 June 2010." The Convention was opened for signature in Rome on 4 November 1950 and came into force on 3 September 1953.

3. Effect of Protocol No. 15 on this presumption

Protocol No. 15 (CETS No. 213), done at Strasbourg on 24 June 2013, in force 1 August 2021, did not amend Article 6. Its operative articles amend only: the Preamble (inserting a recital on subsidiarity and margin of appreciation); Article 21 (judge candidates' age); Article 30 (relinquishment of jurisdiction); and Article 35 (admissibility time-limit and exhaustion). Source: Protocol No. 15 to the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, CETS No. 213, Articles 1–5 (https://www.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/Protocol_15_ENG). The wording of Article 6(2) in the consolidated text presented as amended through Protocol No. 15 is therefore identical to the wording in earlier authentic English texts of the Convention.

4. Training note — what the presumption is, and what it is not

The European Court of Human Rights' Guide on Article 6 (criminal limb) confirms that "Paragraph 2 of Article 6 embodies the principle of the presumption of innocence" and that it requires, inter alia, that (1) members of a court should not start with the preconceived idea that the accused has committed the offence charged; (2) the burden of proof is on the prosecution; and (3) any doubt should benefit the accused (Guide on Article 6 of the Convention – Right to a fair trial (criminal limb), European Court of Human Rights, last update 28 February 2026, § 362, citing Barberà, Messegué and Jabardo v. Spain, 1988, § 77; https://ks.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr-ks/guide_art_6_criminal_eng).

For the training module, the presumption in Article 6(2) should not be conflated with: the privilege against self-incrimination; the Article 6(1) guarantee of a fair and public hearing; or domestic burden-of-proof formulae that use different wording. The Convention text itself does not use the phrase "presumption of innocence" — that label is the Court's and the Guide's name for the guarantee whose operative words are those quoted in section 1 above.

5. Recommended module wording (drop-in)

"Under Article 6(2) of the European Convention on Human Rights, in the text presented as amended through Protocol No. 15: 'Everyone charged with a criminal offence shall be presumed innocent until proved guilty according to law.' This is the presumption of innocence. It applies to everyone charged with a criminal offence within the jurisdiction of the High Contracting Parties."

End of draft. A qualified attorney should confirm the quotation against the current official consolidated text before the module is published, and should decide whether the French authentic text ("Toute personne accusée d'une infraction est présumée innocente jusqu'à ce que sa culpabilité ait été légalement établie") should also be shown for bilingual audiences.

question: Y132
answer:
MEMORANDUM

To: Reviewing Attorney
From: Legal Researcher
Date: 2026-11-21
Re: Combined interval from service of an FTC Part 3 complaint to the scheduling conference, using only the answer period and the post-answer conference period
Jurisdiction: United States — Federal Trade Commission administrative adjudication (16 CFR Part 3)
Status: DRAFT for attorney review; not legal advice

QUESTION

In a single-respondent FTC adjudication under 16 CFR Part 3 as in force on 2026-11-21, the respondent uses the entire answer period, and the Administrative Law Judge then uses the entire period allowed after that answer to hold the scheduling conference. Using only those two stated periods, what is the combined interval from service of the complaint to the conference?

SHORT ANSWER

24 days after service of the complaint.

AUTHORITY AND TEXT

1. Answer period — 14 days.

16 C.F.R. § 3.12(a) (2026) provides: “A respondent shall file an answer within 14 days after being served with the complaint.”

That text is the text in the 2026 annual edition of the CFR (Title 16, Part 3) and on the current eCFR as fetched 2026-11-22. It was adopted at 74 Fed. Reg. 1820, 1820–01 (Jan. 13, 2009). No later final amendment changes this 14-day period.

2. Scheduling-conference period — 10 days after the last answer.

16 C.F.R. § 3.21(b) (2026) provides: “Not later than 10 days after the answer is filed by the last answering respondent, the Administrative Law Judge shall hold a scheduling conference.”

That text is likewise the 2026 CFR / current eCFR text. Section 3.21 was amended at 88 Fed. Reg. 42,875 (July 5, 2023); that amendment did not alter the 10-day conference deadline. The “last answering respondent” language is irrelevant to the interval in a single-respondent case: the last (and only) answer is the one answer.

3. Historical proposals are not the rule in force.

An earlier FTC rulemaking notice proposed a 20-day answer (§ 3.12(a)) and a 14-day conference (§ 3.21(b)), and an even earlier 1996 configuration used a 7-day conference window. Those figures are not the rule as in force on 2026-11-21. The operative numbers are 14 and 10.

CALCULATION

The problem states that both periods are used in full, run consecutively, and are the only periods to be counted. No motion, stay, amended answer, or case-specific order is assumed.

Step 1 — Answer. Under § 3.12(a), counting the day after service as day 1 (the day of service is not counted), the answer is due on the 14th day after service. The respondent files on that 14th day.

Step 2 — Conference. Under § 3.21(b), counting the day after filing as day 1 (the day the answer is filed is not counted), the ALJ holds the conference not later than the 10th day after the answer is filed. The ALJ holds it on that 10th day.

Step 3 — Combined interval. Service (day 0) → answer (day 14) → conference (day 24).

14 days + 10 days = 24 days from service of the complaint to the scheduling conference.

This count uses calendar days and does not add weekend or federal-holiday makeup days. The question directs that only the two stated periods be used. If either deadline fell on a Saturday, Sunday, or federal holiday, a computation-of-time rule could push that single deadline to the next business day and increase the elapsed calendar span; that contingency is outside the two stated periods and is not included in the 24-day figure.

ASSUMPTIONS (stated so they can be checked)

- Governing text is 16 CFR Part 3 as printed in the 2026 CFR annual edition and confirmed on the current eCFR; no amendment effective on or before 2026-11-21 changes § 3.12(a) or § 3.21(b).
- Single respondent, so the § 3.21(b) clock runs from that respondent’s answer.
- Both periods run consecutively and are used in full; there is no overlap, tolling, or extension.
- No motion under § 3.26(d) or other stay is filed (such a motion stays the proceeding and tolls Part 3 deadlines).
- Service of the complaint starts the § 3.12(a) clock on the day after service.

CONCLUSION

Using only the two stated periods, the combined interval from service of the complaint to the scheduling conference is 24 days.

Primary sources: 16 C.F.R. § 3.12(a) (2026); 16 C.F.R. § 3.21(b) (2026); 74 Fed. Reg. 1820 (Jan. 13, 2009); 88 Fed. Reg. 42,875 (July 5, 2023).
cautions: The answer gives 24 days for ask 5, and that figure is in none of the passages found on their pages.

question: Y133
answer:
MEMORANDUM — DRAFT FOR QUALIFIED ATTORNEY REVIEW (not legal advice)

Jurisdiction: European Union (merger control).

1. Governing authority

Council Regulation (EC) No 139/2004 of 20 January 2004 on the control of concentrations between undertakings (the “Merger Regulation”), OJ L 24, 29.1.2004, p. 1.

Article 1(2) provides, in the text published in the Official Journal:

“A concentration has a Community dimension where:
(a) the combined aggregate worldwide turnover of all the undertakings concerned is more than EUR 5 000 million; and
(b) the aggregate Community-wide turnover of each of at least two of the undertakings concerned is more than EUR 250 million,
unless each of the undertakings concerned achieves more than two-thirds of its aggregate Community-wide turnover within one and the same Member State.”

Source: Council Regulation (EC) No 139/2004, Article 1(2), OJ L 24, 29.1.2004, p. 1; text also reproduced at https://wipolex-res.wipo.int/edocs/lexdocs/laws/en/eu/eu104en.html (fetched 2026-11-22).

The thresholds against which the recorded amounts are compared are therefore:
- EUR 5 000 million — combined aggregate worldwide turnover (Article 1(2)(a));
- EUR 250 million — aggregate Community-wide turnover, per undertaking (Article 1(2)(b)).

The sources consulted state these values as the Article 1(2) figures. No amending act changing those two numbers was identified in the material reviewed. Turnover is the concept defined in Article 5 of the same Regulation (OJ L 24, 29.1.2004, p. 1, Article 5).

2. Recorded amounts (as given by the filing team)

- Combined aggregate worldwide turnover of all the undertakings concerned: EUR 5 400 million.
- Aggregate Community-wide turnover of the first undertaking concerned: EUR 300 million.
- Aggregate Community-wide turnover of the second undertaking concerned: EUR 275 million.

3. Arithmetic overage — the only question asked

The Regulation’s test is “more than” each threshold, so the relevant comparison is recorded amount minus threshold. Each result is positive, i.e. each recorded amount is strictly greater than the corresponding statutory figure.

(a) Combined aggregate worldwide turnover — Article 1(2)(a)
Recorded: EUR 5 400 million
Threshold: EUR 5 000 million
Excess: 5 400 − 5 000 = EUR 400 million

(b) Aggregate Community-wide turnover, first undertaking — Article 1(2)(b)
Recorded: EUR 300 million
Threshold: EUR 250 million
Excess: 300 − 250 = EUR 50 million

(c) Aggregate Community-wide turnover, second undertaking — Article 1(2)(b)
Recorded: EUR 275 million
Threshold: EUR 250 million
Excess: 275 − 250 = EUR 25 million

Answer to the ask: the recorded amounts exceed the corresponding Article 1(2) thresholds by EUR 400 million (worldwide), EUR 50 million (Community-wide, first undertaking) and EUR 25 million (Community-wide, second undertaking).

4. What this memorandum expressly does not decide

As instructed, this memorandum does not decide, and must not be read as deciding, whether the concentration has a Community dimension. In particular:
- the final clause of Article 1(2) (more than two-thirds of aggregate Community-wide turnover achieved in one and the same Member State) is not applied;
- Article 1(3) (alternative Community-dimension thresholds) is not applied;
- no conclusion is drawn that the numerical overages in section 3 do, or do not, give the concentration a Community dimension.

5. Assumptions on which the arithmetic rests (for reviewer confirmation)

- The recorded figures are stated in EUR millions and are comparable to the Article 1(2) thresholds without adjustment (in particular, they are taken to be turnover as defined in Article 5 of the Merger Regulation, OJ L 24, 29.1.2004, p. 1, Article 5 — net of VAT and intra-undertaking sales).
- The two Community-wide figures relate to two undertakings concerned in the same concentration, so each is compared to the Article 1(2)(b) per-undertaking threshold of EUR 250 million.
- The applicable version of Article 1(2) is the text quoted in section 1 (EUR 5 000 million / EUR 250 million). If a different amendment state applies at the relevant filing date, the subtraction must be re-run against that version’s numbers.
- Only the arithmetic overage is requested; no proportionality, combined-Community-wide, or Member State allocation analysis is performed.

question: Y134
answer:

MEMORANDUM

Jurisdiction: European Union (Directive 2011/83/EU). The optional exclusion is exercised Member State by Member State; no national implementing statute is identified in the instruction. The analysis below is EU-law level on the Directive text as framed by the question. National transposition must be checked before reliance in any given Member State.

Questions
1. What total is used for the EUR 50 threshold when a consumer simultaneously concludes two off-premises contracts with related subjects requiring payments of EUR 30 and EUR 25?
2. Does the optional off-premises exclusion, taken at the maximum EUR 50 value, cover this pair on that basis?

Short answers
1. The combined total of EUR 55 (EUR 30 + EUR 25).
2. No. The optional exclusion does not cover the pair, because the aggregated payment of EUR 55 exceeds the EUR 50 ceiling of the option as exercised at its maximum.

Governing provisions (primary sources, cited in full)

Directive 2011/83/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 25 October 2011 on consumer rights, amending Council Directive 93/13/EEC and Directive 1999/44/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council and repealing Council Directive 85/577/EEC and Directive 97/7/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council, OJ L 304, 22.11.2011, p. 64–88 (CELEX 32011L0083).

Optional exclusion (operative text). Article 3(3) provides:
"Member States may decide not to apply this Directive or not to maintain or introduce corresponding national provisions to off-premises contracts for which the payment to be made by the consumer does not exceed EUR 50. Member States may define a lower value in their national legislation."
(The same text appears as the fourth paragraph of Article 3 in the legislation.gov.uk rendering of the Directive; the Official Journal text numbers it Article 3(3).) Source: Directive 2011/83/EU, Art. 3(3), OJ L 304, 22.11.2011, p. 64–88; also at https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32011L0083 and https://www.legislation.gov.uk/eudr/2011/83.

Aggregation rule (recital). Recital 28 provides:
"In order to avoid administrative burden being placed on traders, Member States may decide not to apply this Directive where goods or services of a minor value are sold off-premises. The monetary threshold should be established at a sufficiently low level as to exclude only purchases of small significance. Member States should be allowed to define this value in their national legislation provided that it does not exceed EUR 50. Where two or more contracts with related subjects are concluded at the same time by the consumer, the total cost thereof should be taken into account for the purpose of applying this threshold."
Source: Directive 2011/83/EU, Recital 28, OJ L 304, 22.11.2011, p. 64–88.

Definition. An "off-premises contract" is defined in Article 2(8) as any contract between the trader and the consumer concluded in the simultaneous physical presence of the parties in a place which is not the trader's business premises (and the related offer/after-contact limbs). Source: Directive 2011/83/EU, Art. 2(8), OJ L 304, 22.11.2011, p. 64–88.

Application to the facts

The question stipulates that (i) the Member State has exercised the Article 3(3) option at the maximum EUR 50 value, (ii) both contracts are off-premises contracts, (iii) they are concluded simultaneously, (iv) they have related subjects, and (v) the figures EUR 30 and EUR 25 are the payments/total prices, without incidental charges that would alter the arithmetic.

Threshold total. Recital 28 directs that where two or more contracts with related subjects are concluded at the same time, "the total cost thereof should be taken into account." The relevant figure is therefore the combined payment, not each contract assessed separately:

EUR 30 + EUR 25 = EUR 55.

Coverage. Article 3(3) permits Member States not to apply the Directive to off-premises contracts "for which the payment to be made by the consumer does not exceed EUR 50." "Does not exceed" is a ceiling of EUR 50 inclusive. EUR 55 exceeds EUR 50. The optional exclusion therefore does not cover this pair. Each contract taken alone (EUR 30 and EUR 25) would fall inside a EUR 50 threshold; the aggregation rule in Recital 28 is what prevents that split result, and it applies on the facts as given (simultaneous conclusion; related subjects).

Verdict on ask 2: not covered.

Where authority is thin or requires confirmation

1. Recital versus operative article. The aggregation rule appears in Recital 28, not in the operative text of Article 3(3). Recitals are a standard CJEU interpretive aid and this one is specific and unambiguous, but a national court applying only the operative words of a transposing statute could in theory read Article 3(3) contract-by-contract. The national transposition should be checked to confirm it reproduces (or that national interpretation accepts) the aggregation rule.

2. No national statute identified. The option is national-law-by-national-law, and a Member State may set a value lower than EUR 50. The question stipulates the maximum EUR 50 is used. If the actual Member State set a lower figure, both contracts could still be outside the exclusion even without aggregation (any threshold below EUR 25), or the outcome could differ at the margin. The implementing statute for the relevant Member State has not been supplied.

3. No CJEU judgment on this aggregation rule is in the record. The conclusion rests on the Directive text itself.

4. "Total price" / "payment to be made." Article 3(3) refers to "the payment to be made by the consumer"; Recital 28 refers to "total cost." The analysis assumes the stipulated figures of EUR 30 and EUR 25 are those amounts. Taxes, delivery or surcharges that form part of the payment would increase the combined figure and would not bring the pair back inside EUR 50.

5. "Related subjects." The question states the contracts have related subjects. The Directive does not define that phrase. If the subjects were not related, Recital 28 would not aggregate them and each contract would be tested separately (EUR 30 and EUR 25, both ≤ EUR 50, both potentially excluded).

Conclusion

Under Directive 2011/83/EU, where a Member State has taken the Article 3(3) optional off-premises exclusion at the maximum EUR 50 value, the total used for the threshold in respect of two simultaneously concluded related-subject contracts of EUR 30 and EUR 25 is EUR 55. On that basis the optional exclusion does not cover the pair, because EUR 55 exceeds EUR 50.

This memorandum is a draft for review by a qualified attorney. It is not legal advice and should not be relied on until the applicable national transposition has been identified and checked.
cautions: The answer gives 55 EUR for ask 1, and that figure is in none of the passages found on their pages.

MEMORANDUM

To: Reviewing attorney
From: Legal researcher
Re: Status of the Appendix of Forms to the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, as amended through December 1, 2025, and the effective date of the change
Jurisdiction: United States federal courts (federal civil procedure only; no state analogue is addressed)

1. Questions presented

A 2014 litigation manual directs users to the Appendix of Forms in the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure. In the rules as amended to December 1, 2025, what is that appendix's status, and when did the change take effect?

2. Short answers

Status (Ask 2): Abrogated. Rule 84 and the Appendix of Forms no longer exist as part of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure. They were abrogated as part of the 2015 civil-rules amendment package and have not been restored in any later edition, including the edition effective December 1, 2025.

Effective date (Ask 3): December 1, 2015. That is the date the abrogation took effect. It is not December 1, 2025; the latter date is only the "as amended through" date specified in the request (the most recent amendment cycle of the Civil Rules).

3. Analysis

(a) What the 2014 manual was pointing to. Until December 1, 2015, Rule 84 provided: "The forms contained in the Appendix of Forms are sufficient under the rules and are intended to indicate the simplicity and brevity of statement which the rules contemplate. [As amended Dec. 27, 1946, eff. Mar. 19, 1948.]" Historical text retrieved from the Northern District of Illinois rules archive: https://www.ilnd.uscourts.gov/_assets/_documents/_forms/_legal//frcpweb/FRC00090.HTM (fetched 2026-11-22). A manual written in 2014 was, at the time it was written, consistent with then-current law.

(b) The abrogation. The Federal Judicial Center's rules announcement for Fed. R. Civ. P. 84 states: "Amendments to the following Federal Rules of Civil Procedure became effective on December 1, 2015: 1, 4, 16, 26, 30, 31, 33, 34, 37, and 55. Rule 84 and the Appendix of Forms were abrogated." The same page records that the package was transmitted to Congress on April 29, 2015, "concerning amendments to the Federal Rules of Practice and Procedure to become effective on December 1, 2015." Federal Judicial Center, Amendments to the Federal Rules of Practice and Procedure 2015—Civil Rules Redline, https://www.fjc.gov/federal-rules-practice-and-procedure/fed.-r.-civil-p.-84 (fetched 2026-11-22).

(c) Effective-date mechanism. Amendments to the civil rules adopted by the Supreme Court take effect no later than December 1 of the year of transmittal unless Congress otherwise provides by law. 28 U.S.C. § 2074(a). The April 29, 2015 transmittal and the December 1, 2015 effective date recorded by the FJC are consistent with that statute. The fetched materials do not include the text of the Supreme Court's April 29, 2015 order itself; the reviewing attorney should confirm the order number and the Committee Note to the abrogation of Rule 84 against the official 2015 rules package before the manual correction is published.

(d) Status as of the December 1, 2025 edition. The Administrative Office / Judicial Conference current-rules page states that the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure "were last amended in 2025" and offers the "Federal Rules of Civil Procedure Pamphlet, Dec. 1, 2025" as the current official text. https://www.uscourts.gov/forms-rules/current-rules-practice-procedure/federal-rules-civil-procedure (fetched 2026-11-22). Abrogation is a removal from the rules. Nothing in the fetched materials suggests Rule 84 or the Appendix of Forms was restored after 2015. Accordingly, in the rules as amended to December 1, 2025, the Appendix of Forms remains abrogated and is not part of the official rules. The reviewing attorney should visually confirm against the official December 1, 2025 pamphlet that neither Rule 84 nor an Appendix of Forms appears; the fetched current-rules landing page confirms the 2025 edition but does not reproduce the full text of every rule.

(e) What the appendix is not. The Appendix of Forms to the Civil Rules is distinct from (i) the national federal court forms now hosted by the Administrative Office at uscourts.gov/forms, (ii) the Supplemental Rules' admiralty forms, and (iii) any local-court forms. A 2014 manual that cites "the Appendix of Forms" in the FRCP is citing the abrogated rules appendix, not the Administrative Office civil forms collection. The uscourts.gov page separately advertises "national federal court form[s] that can be used in all federal courts," which is the successor practical resource, not a continuation of the abrogated appendix. https://www.uscourts.gov/forms-rules/current-rules-practice-procedure/federal-rules-civil-procedure (fetched 2026-11-22).

4. Flagged correction to the 2014 manual

Do not rewrite the manual in this draft. Flag for the reviewing attorney:

• Delete or replace every direction to "Appendix of Forms," "Form No. __ of the Appendix of Forms," or "Rule 84." Those citations have been erroneous since December 1, 2015.
• Replacement language, subject to attorney approval: "Rule 84 and the Appendix of Forms to the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure were abrogated effective December 1, 2015. See Fed. R. Civ. P. 84 (abrogated 2015); Amendments to the Federal Rules of Practice and Procedure 2015—Civil Rules Redline (FJC). Sufficient form is no longer prescribed by a rules appendix. National forms are available from the Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts, and pleading sufficiency is governed by Rules 1, 8, and 10."
• If the manual cites a specific numbered form (e.g., Form 1A complaint), the correction should identify a successor Administrative Office form or state that no official rules-form successor exists. The fetched materials do not include a form-by-form concordance; that mapping is left to the reviewing attorney.
• No transitional or savings provision preserving use of the old appendix forms in pending cases appears in the fetched materials. The default is that the abrogation applied from December 1, 2015. If the manual's audience includes cases in which a court had already ordered use of an appendix form, that case-specific order, not the appendix, would control.

5. Authority assessment

The FJC statement is explicit on both the status ("Rule 84 and the Appendix of Forms were abrogated") and the date ("effective on December 1, 2015"). The FJC is an agency of the federal judiciary and a reliable secondary/official-adjacent source, but it is not itself the amending order. Thin or not in the fetched set: (i) the Supreme Court order of April 29, 2015; (ii) the 2015 Committee Note explaining the Advisory Committee's rationale; (iii) page-by-page confirmation that the December 1, 2025 pamphlet omits Rule 84. None of those gaps changes the answer; they are listed so the reviewing attorney can complete the citation file. Sources consulted in the research set:

• Federal Judicial Center, Fed. R. Civ. P. 84 announcement, https://www.fjc.gov/federal-rules-practice-and-procedure/fed.-r.-civil-p.-84 (fetched 2026-11-22T23:51:06Z).
• U.S. Courts, Federal Rules of Civil Procedure (current rules landing page; pamphlet Dec. 1, 2025), https://www.uscourts.gov/forms-rules/current-rules-practice-procedure/federal-rules-civil-procedure (fetched 2026-11-22T23:51:06Z).
• Historical Rule 84 text, N.D. Ill. rules archive, https://www.ilnd.uscourts.gov/_assets/_documents/_forms/_legal//frcpweb/FRC00090.HTM (fetched 2026-11-22T23:51:06Z).
• U.S. Code, Title 28 Appendix (preliminary edition) node referenced at https://uscodehouse.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title28a-node89 (fetched but not quoted in the passage set; not relied on for a holding).
• Justia reproduction of former Rule 84, https://law.justia.com/codes/us/title-28/appendix/federal-rules-of-civil-procedure/content-1234/rule-84/ (listed in the source set; historical/commercial reprint, not treated as controlling).

6. Controlling-source decision (stated because it was unspecified)

The controlling text is treated as the official Federal Rules of Civil Procedure published by the Judicial Conference / Administrative Office, currently the pamphlet dated December 1, 2025, as authorized under 28 U.S.C. §§ 2071–2072, 2074. Commercial reprints (Justia and similar) and archived district-court copies (N.D. Ill.) are used only as historical evidence of pre-abrogation text.

7. Bottom line for the values reported

Ask 2 — status: abrogated.
Ask 3 — effective date: December 1, 2015 (reported as 2015-12-01).
Constraint (Ask 1): the foregoing is stated for the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure as amended through December 1, 2025, United States federal courts.

MEMORANDUM

To: Reviewing attorney
From: Legal researcher
Re: Term of office and re-election of judges of the European Court of Human Rights — Convention as amended through Protocol No. 15
Jurisdiction: Council of Europe / Convention system (not any domestic jurisdiction)
Status: Draft for review. This memorandum is not legal advice.

I. QUESTIONS PRESENTED

An internal training slide states that judges of the European Court of Human Rights serve “renewable six-year terms.” Against the Convention text presented as amended through Protocol No. 15:

1. What is the term for which judges are elected?
2. May a judge be re-elected?

II. SHORT ANSWERS

1. Election term: nine years.
2. Re-election: No. Judges may not be re-elected.

The slide is inaccurate as to the current treaty text. “Renewable six-year terms” was the rule under the Convention as amended by Protocol No. 11 (ETS No. 155), in force as the Court’s governing structure from 1 November 1998 until 1 June 2010. It is not the rule in the Convention as amended through Protocol No. 15.

III. GOVERNING AUTHORITY — PRIMARY TEXT, CITED IN FULL

A. The provision as it stands

Instrument: Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, as amended by Protocol No. 11 (ETS No. 155, 11.V.1994), Protocol No. 14 (CETS No. 194, 13.V.2004) and Protocol No. 15 (CETS No. 213, 24.X.2013).

Official text used: the English text published by the Court, “The text of the Convention is presented as amended by the provisions of Protocol No. 15 (CETS No. 213) as from its entry into force on 1 August 2021 and of Protocol No. 14 (CETS No. 194) as from its entry into force on 1 June 2010.” Only the English and French versions are authentic.

Source URL: https://www.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/Convention_eng (fetched 2026-11-22).

Article 23 — Terms of office and dismissal (current text, quoted in full):

“ARTICLE 23
Terms of office and dismissal
1. The judges shall be elected for a period of nine years. They may not be re-elected.
2. The judges shall hold office until replaced. They shall, however, continue to deal with such cases as they already have under consideration.
3. No judge may be dismissed from office unless the other judges decide by a majority of two-thirds that that judge has ceased to fulfil the required conditions.”

The operative words for both questions are in Article 23, paragraph 1: “The judges shall be elected for a period of nine years. They may not be re-elected.”

B. The amending instrument that changed the term (Protocol No. 14)

Instrument: Protocol No. 14 to the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, amending the control system of the Convention, CETS No. 194, signed 13 May 2004, in force 1 June 2010.

Source URL: https://www.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/library_collection_p14_ets194e_eng

Article 2 of Protocol No. 14 replaced Article 23 of the Convention with the following (quoted in full):

“Article 23 – Terms of office and dismissal
1 The judges shall be elected for a period of nine years. They may not be re-elected.
2 The terms of office of judges shall expire when they reach the age of 70.
3 The judges shall hold office until replaced. They shall, however, continue to deal with such cases as they already have under consideration.
4 No judge may be dismissed from office unless the other judges decide by a majority of two-thirds that that judge has ceased to fulfil the required conditions.”

Protocol No. 14 also contained a transitional extension (Article 21): first-term judges then serving had their terms extended ipso jure to a total of nine years; other judges completed a term extended ipso jure by two years. That transition is spent.

C. Protocol No. 15 — what it did and did not do to Article 23

Instrument: Protocol No. 15 amending the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, CETS No. 213, in force 1 August 2021.

Explanatory Report source URL: https://www.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/Protocol_15_explanatory_report_ENG

Protocol No. 15 did not reopen the nine-year / non-re-election rule. Its amendments relevant to judges concerned Article 21 (a new age-65 ceiling for candidates at the date the three-candidate list is requested) and the deletion of the former Article 23(2) age-70 cessation rule (so that, in the current consolidated text, former paragraphs 3 and 4 of Article 23 were renumbered as paragraphs 2 and 3).

The Explanatory Report to Protocol No. 15, paragraphs 11–12, states:

“A new paragraph 2 is introduced in order to require that candidates be less than 65 years of age at the date by which the list of three candidates has been requested by the Parliamentary Assembly further to its role in electing judges under Article 22 of the Convention.”

“This modification aims at enabling highly qualified judges to serve the full nine-year term of office and thereby reinforce the consistency of the membership of the Court. The age limit applied under Article 23, paragraph 2 of the Convention, as drafted prior to the entry into force of this Protocol, had the effect of preventing certain experienced judges from completing their term of office. It was considered no longer essential to impose an age limit, given the fact that judges’ terms of office are no longer renewable.”

The phrase “the full nine-year term of office” and the statement that “judges’ terms of office are no longer renewable” independently confirm both answers.

D. The superseded text that the training slide reflects (Protocol No. 11)

Instrument: Protocol No. 11 to the Convention, ETS No. 155, signed 11 May 1994, in force 1 November 1998 (restructuring; single permanent Court).

Source URL: https://www.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/library_collection_p11_ets155e_eng

Former Article 23, paragraph 1 (quoted in full):

“Article 23 – Terms of office
1 The judges shall be elected for a period of six years. They may be re-elected. However, the terms of office of one-half of the judges elected at the first election shall expire at the end of three years.”

That is the textual source of “renewable six-year terms.” It has not been the law of the Convention since Protocol No. 14 entered into force on 1 June 2010.

IV. ANALYSIS

The constraint in the request is the Convention “as amended through Protocol No. 15.” The official consolidated English text satisfying that constraint is the Court’s published edition noted in Section III.A. In that text, Article 23(1) is express on both points. There is no judicial decision needed to interpret it; the words are unqualified. “Nine years” is the election term. “They may not be re-elected” is a prohibition, not a permission, and it is not subject to any stated exception for casual vacancies, sitting judges, or any other category.

Related provisions do not alter those two answers. Article 22 (election by the Parliamentary Assembly from lists of three candidates) concerns who elects and on what list; it says nothing about term length or re-election. Article 25 (as now numbered) provides that the President, Vice-Presidents and Presidents of Chambers are elected for three years and “may be re-elected”; that re-election language applies to those offices, not to judgeship as such, and it is a different provision. Continuation in office under Article 23(2) (“hold office until replaced” and finish cases already under consideration) is not re-election.

Protocol No. 16 (CETS No. 214) is outside the requested “through Protocol No. 15” frame. It does not amend Article 23. It is noted only to confirm it was not omitted because it would change the result.

V. CORRECTION TO THE TRAINING SLIDE (proposed wording)

Replace the slide statement with:

“Judges of the European Court of Human Rights are elected for a single, non-renewable term of nine years. They may not be re-elected. Authority: Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, Article 23(1), as amended by Protocol No. 14 (CETS No. 194) and as presented as amended through Protocol No. 15 (CETS No. 213, in force 1 August 2021). The former renewable six-year term (Protocol No. 11, former Article 23(1), ETS No. 155) ceased to apply when Protocol No. 14 entered into force on 1 June 2010.”

VI. SCOPE, AUTHORITY QUALITY, AND LIMITS

• Jurisdiction named: Council of Europe / European Convention on Human Rights system. No domestic-law analysis is included, and none is needed for these two questions.
• Primary sources: the treaty texts themselves, quoted above. The Explanatory Report to Protocol No. 15 is used only as confirmatory context for what Protocol No. 15 did to Article 23; the binding rule is the Convention text.
• Authenticity: only the English and French versions of the Convention are authentic. This memorandum cites the English authentic text.
• Authority is not thin or conflicting on these two questions. The current Article 23(1), the Protocol No. 14 amending text, and the Protocol No. 15 Explanatory Report all agree. The only “conflict” is historical: the slide recites the superseded Protocol No. 11 rule.
• This draft has not been reviewed by a qualified attorney and is not legal advice.

VII. RESULT VALUES (as requested)

Ask 2 (election term): 9 years.
Ask 3 (may a judge be re-elected?): No.
