question: Y137
answer:
DRAFT FOR ATTORNEY REVIEW — NOT LEGAL ADVICE

JURISDICTION: European Union (State aid, Articles 107 and 108 TFEU).

MEMORANDUM

To: Reviewing attorney
From: Legal researcher
Re: Whether Commission Regulation (EU) No 651/2014 (GBER) can exempt from notification aid to facilitate the closure of an uncompetitive coal mine, and the instrument the GBER identifies as governing that aid

1. QUESTIONS PRESENTED

1. Can a State-aid team rely on Commission Regulation (EU) No 651/2014 to exempt aid to facilitate the closure of an uncompetitive coal mine from notification?
2. If not, which instrument does the Regulation's scope passage identify as dealing with that aid?

2. SHORT ANSWERS

1. No.
2. Council Decision of 10 December 2010 on State aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines (2010/787/EU).

3. ANALYSIS

3.1 What the GBER is, and why the question is one of scope

Commission Regulation (EU) No 651/2014 of 17 June 2014 declaring certain categories of aid compatible with the internal market in application of Articles 107 and 108 of the Treaty (Text with EEA relevance) [OJ L 187, 26.6.2014, p. 1] (the 'GBER') is a block-exemption regulation. Recital (7) states: 'Aid that fulfils all the conditions laid down in this Regulation both general and specific to the relevant categories of aid should be exempted from the notification obligation laid down in Article 108(3) of the Treaty.' [GBER, recital 7.] Reliance on the GBER is therefore an exemption from prior notification under Article 108(3) TFEU [Consolidated Version of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, OJ C 202, 10.6.2016, p. 47]. If the GBER does not apply, that exemption is not available.

3.2 The GBER's scope passage expressly carves out coal-mine closure aid and names the alternative instrument

The scope passage is unambiguous. Recital (12) of the GBER states:

'This Regulation should not apply to aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines, which is dealt with by the Council Decision of 10 December 2010 on State aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines(6). This Regulation should apply to other types of aid in the coal sector, with the exception of regional aid.' [GBER, recital 12.]

The operative scope provision repeats the exclusion and identifies the same instrument by number. The consulted text of Article 1 lists among the categories to which the GBER does not apply:

'(d) aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines, as covered by Council Decision No 2010/787;' [GBER, art. 1.]

(In the original 2014 Official Journal text this exclusion appears as Article 1(3)(a); later consolidations renumber the same exclusion. The words are the same in substance.)

The GBER also defines 'coal' by cross-reference to that same Decision: "'coal' means high-grade, medium-grade and low-grade category A and B coal within the meaning of the international codification system for coal established by the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe and clarified in the Council decision of 10 December 2010 on State aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines" [GBER, art. 2(13)].

On the face of the Regulation's own scope passage, the answer to question 1 is therefore No: a State-aid team cannot rely on the GBER to exempt this aid from notification. The answer to question 2 is the Council Decision of 10 December 2010, known as Council Decision No 2010/787/EU [Council Decision of 10 December 2010 on State aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines (2010/787/EU), OJ L 336, 7.12.2010, p. 28].

Note on the instrument's nature: it is a Council Decision, not a Commission Decision. Internal notes describing it as 'Commission Decision No 2010/787/EU' should be corrected.

3.3 What the identified instrument is — and what it is not

Council Decision 2010/787/EU is a compatibility framework, not a block exemption from notification. Its Article 2(1) provides: 'In the context of closure of uncompetitive mines, aid to the coal industry may be considered compatible with the proper functioning of the internal market if it complies with the provisions of this Decision.' [Decision 2010/787/EU, art. 2(1).] The Decision's recitals contemplate that measures will be notified: 'The Commission should assess the measures notified on the basis of this Decision and take decisions in accordance with Council Regulation (EC) No 659/1999.' [Decision 2010/787/EU, recital on assessment.] Switching from the GBER to this Decision therefore does not solve a notification problem. Aid under the Decision must be notified under Article 108(3) TFEU and assessed by the Commission.

The Decision's principal operative conditions, as they appear in the consulted text, are:

- Closure aid (Article 3): aid intended specifically to cover current production losses of coal production units may be considered compatible only if, among other conditions, 'the operation of the coal production units concerned must form part of a closure plan the deadline of which does not extend beyond 31 December 2018' and 'the coal production units concerned must be closed definitively in accordance with the closure plan'. If the units are not closed at the authorised date, the Member State 'shall recover all aid granted in respect of the whole period covered by the closure plan'. [Decision 2010/787/EU, art. 3(1)(a), (b) and art. 3(3).]
- Aid to cover exceptional costs (Article 4): aid to cover costs arising from closure that are not related to current production may be considered compatible, limited to defined Annex cost categories, and does not apply to costs resulting from non-compliance with environmental regulations. [Decision 2010/787/EU, art. 4.]
- Duration: 'It shall apply from 1 January 2011. It shall expire on 31 December 2027.' [Decision 2010/787/EU, final article.]

3.4 Temporal and definitional caveats (not needed to answer the two asks, but material to advice)

The two asks are what the GBER permits and what the GBER names. Those answers do not depend on whether Decision 2010/787/EU is still a live route. For completeness:

- The Article 3 closure-aid route required a closure-plan deadline no later than 31 December 2018. A new closure after that date cannot rely on Article 3. Article 4 exceptional-costs aid may remain theoretically available for qualifying closure costs until the Decision expires on 31 December 2027, subject to its own conditions. [Decision 2010/787/EU, arts. 3 and 4, and final article.]
- The carve-out and the Decision are limited to 'uncompetitive coal mines'. If the undertaking is not a hard-coal production unit meeting the Decision's criteria (for example lignite, or a mine that is not 'uncompetitive' as defined), the GBER exclusion and the Decision may not be the right frame at all, and a different analysis would be required. [GBER, recital 12 and art. 1; Decision 2010/787/EU, art. 1 definitions.]
- Recital (12) of the GBER adds that the Regulation 'should apply to other types of aid in the coal sector, with the exception of regional aid'. If a proposed measure contains discrete components that are not 'aid to facilitate the closure' (for example environmental-protection investment, innovation, or training that would qualify under other GBER headings), those components may separately be assessed against the GBER. The closure-facilitation aid itself cannot be. [GBER, recital 12.]

3.5 Consequence of relying on the GBER for this aid

If the team treats the GBER as applying when Article 1 excludes the aid, any grant would be implemented without a valid notification exemption. If the measure is State aid within Article 107(1) TFEU, non-notification breaches Article 108(3) TFEU, the aid is unlawful, and the Commission may open proceedings and order recovery under Article 108(2) TFEU. [TFEU, arts. 107(1), 108(2) and 108(3), OJ C 202, 10.6.2016, p. 47.]

4. CONCLUSIONS

1. No. Commission Regulation (EU) No 651/2014 cannot be relied on to exempt aid to facilitate the closure of an uncompetitive coal mine from notification. The Regulation excludes that aid from its scope. [GBER, recital 12 and art. 1, OJ L 187, 26.6.2014, p. 1.]
2. The instrument identified by the Regulation's scope passage is Council Decision No 2010/787/EU of 10 December 2010 on State aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines [OJ L 336, 7.12.2010, p. 28]. That Decision is a compatibility framework requiring notification; it is not itself a notification exemption. Its Article 3 closure-aid route required closure by 31 December 2018; the Decision expires on 31 December 2027.

PRIMARY SOURCES

1. Commission Regulation (EU) No 651/2014 of 17 June 2014 declaring certain categories of aid compatible with the internal market in application of Articles 107 and 108 of the Treaty (Text with EEA relevance), OJ L 187, 26.6.2014, p. 1–74 — recitals 7 and 12; Article 1 (scope exclusion); Article 2(13) (definition of 'coal').
2. Council Decision of 10 December 2010 on State aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines (2010/787/EU), OJ L 336, 7.12.2010, p. 28–29 — recitals; Articles 1–4; final article (application from 1 January 2011; expiry 31 December 2027).
3. Consolidated Version of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, OJ C 202, 10.6.2016, p. 47 — Articles 107(1), 108(2), 108(3) and 108(4).

Texts were read in the versions published at legislation.gov.uk (GBER 'adopted' text; Decision 2010/787/EU point-in-time texts of 10 December 2010 and 31 January 2020) and the EUR-Lex consolidated GBER of 27 July 2020. The answers rest on the Official Journal texts cited above, not on secondary commentary.

END OF DRAFT — for review by a qualified attorney. This memorandum is not legal advice.

question: Y138
answer:
MEMORANDUM — DRAFT FOR QUALIFIED ATTORNEY REVIEW — NOT LEGAL ADVICE

Jurisdiction: Council of Europe / Contracting States to the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR). This memorandum addresses the Convention as an international instrument; it does not address any single State's domestic implementation.

QUESTION

A Contracting State invokes Article 15 of the ECHR (derogation in time of emergency) during a war.

1. May it derogate from Article 3 under that provision?
2. What narrow Article 2 exception does the same non-derogation clause state?

SHORT ANSWERS

1. No. Article 3 is expressly non-derogable. Article 15(2) lists Article 3 among the provisions from which "[n]o derogation ... shall be made under this provision." A war or other public emergency, however grave, does not open any derogation from the prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.

2. The sole exception stated for Article 2 is "deaths resulting from lawful acts of war." That is the entire exception. It is narrower than Article 2 as a whole and does not authorise derogation from Article 2(1) generally, nor from the Article 2(2) law-enforcement thresholds (self-defence, lawful arrest, quelling riot or insurrection).

GOVERNING TEXT

Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, Article 15 (Derogation in time of emergency), as published by the European Court of Human Rights (official Convention text, Convention_ENG):

"1. In time of war or other public emergency threatening the life of the nation any High Contracting Party may take measures derogating from its obligations under this Convention to the extent strictly required by the exigencies of the situation, provided that such measures are not inconsistent with its other obligations under international law.

2. No derogation from Article 2, except in respect of deaths resulting from lawful acts of war, or from Articles 3, 4 (paragraph 1) and 7 shall be made under this provision.

3. Any High Contracting Party availing itself of this right of derogation shall keep the Secretary General of the Council of Europe fully informed of the measures which it has taken and the reasons therefor. It shall also inform the Secretary General of the Council of Europe when such measures have ceased to operate and the provisions of the Convention are again being fully executed."

Source (primary, cited in full): European Court of Human Rights, Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, Article 15, https://www.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/Convention_ENG (fetched 2026-11-23).

ANALYSIS

A. Ask 1 — Derogation from Article 3

The operative words of Article 15(2) are a flat prohibition: "No derogation from ... Articles 3, 4 (paragraph 1) and 7 shall be made under this provision." There is no emergency exception, no war exception, and no balancing qualifier attached to Article 3. Article 15(1)'s opening permission ("any High Contracting Party may take measures derogating from its obligations under this Convention") is expressly cut back by Article 15(2). The structure is: paragraph 1 states the general derogation power; paragraph 2 removes specified rights from that power. Article 3 is in the removed list.

The official Court Guide on Article 15 states the same, without qualification:

"Article 15 § 2 protects certain rights from derogation. According to the text of Article 15 § 2, these are: Article 2 (the right to life), except in respect of deaths resulting from lawful acts of war; Article 3 (the prohibition of torture and other forms of ill-treatment); Article 4 § 1 (the prohibition of slavery or servitude); and Article 7 (no punishment without law)."

Source (official Court publication): European Court of Human Rights, Guide on Article 15 of the Convention – Derogation in time of emergency, § 38, https://ks.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr-ks/guide_art_15_eng-pdf (last update 31.08.2026; fetched 2026-11-23).

The Court's official Factsheet on derogation repeats the same list and expressly glosses Article 3 as the "prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment," with no emergency carve-out.

Source (official Court publication): European Court of Human Rights, Factsheet – Derogation in time of emergency, https://prd-echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/FS_Derogation_ENG (February 2022; fetched 2026-11-23).

Consequence: even if the State has lawfully proclaimed a war or other public emergency threatening the life of the nation (Article 15(1)), has notified the Secretary General (Article 15(3)), and has confined itself to measures strictly required by the exigencies of the situation, it still may not derogate from Article 3. Any measure of torture or inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment remains a breach of the Convention. Article 3 is absolute in this framework.

Reinforcement from the Protocols (not the direct answer, but confirms the design): Protocol No. 13 (complete abolition of the death penalty) contains its own non-derogation clause — "No derogation from this Article shall be made under Article 15 of the Convention" (Protocol No. 13, Article 2, as reproduced in the official Convention compilation). Protocol No. 6 likewise bars derogation from its provisions under Article 15 (Protocol No. 6, Article 3). Protocol No. 7, Article 4 § 3, bars derogation from the ne bis in idem rule. None of these creates an Article 3 derogation power; they close further doors.

B. Ask 2 — The narrow Article 2 exception

The same sentence of Article 15(2) states one exception, and only one, to the non-derogation of Article 2:

"except in respect of deaths resulting from lawful acts of war"

That is the identifier. Its scope, on the text:

- It is confined to deaths. It is not a general derogation from the right to life.
- It is confined to deaths resulting from lawful acts of war. "Lawful" looks to both domestic law and the State's other international-law obligations (the Article 15(1) proviso that measures "are not inconsistent with its other obligations under international law" continues to apply). Acts of war that violate international humanitarian law (for example, the Geneva Conventions) are not "lawful acts of war" for this purpose, and deaths they cause are not within the exception.
- It is confined to war. It is not available in a non-war public emergency (the "other public emergency threatening the life of the nation" limb of Article 15(1)).
- It is distinct from, and narrower than, the law-enforcement thresholds in Article 2(2) of the Convention (deprivation of life resulting from the use of force which is no more than absolutely necessary in defence of any person from unlawful violence; lawful arrest; action lawfully taken for the purpose of quelling a riot or insurrection). Article 15(2) does not reopen those, and it does not treat them as a derogation power.

The Court Guide restates the exception in identical words: "Article 2 (the right to life), except in respect of deaths resulting from lawful acts of war." Factsheet: "the right to life, except in the context of lawful acts of war."

C. Assumptions (stated because no named State or conflict was given)

- The analysis reads Articles 2, 3 and 15 from the Convention text itself, not from any one High Contracting Party's domestic law.
- The "war" scenario is treated as within Article 15(1)'s first limb ("In time of war"), so the threshold existence of an Article 15(1) situation is assumed satisfied for the purpose of this memorandum. Nothing in that assumption creates an Article 3 derogation power.
- No specific derogation notice, measure, or detainee-treatment fact pattern is before the writer. If a concrete measure is later identified (for example, interrogation methods, conditions of detention, or removals), the Article 3 conclusion remains: those cannot be saved by Article 15.

D. Authority

Primary (controlling text):
Council of Europe / European Court of Human Rights, Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, Article 15 §§ 1–3, and Articles 2 and 3, official English text, https://www.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/Convention_ENG.

Official Court publications confirming the reading (not independent sources of law, but official explanations of the same text):
- Guide on Article 15 of the Convention – Derogation in time of emergency, §§ 1–4, 38–39, https://ks.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr-ks/guide_art_15_eng-pdf.
- Factsheet – Derogation in time of emergency, https://prd-echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/FS_Derogation_ENG.

No conflicting authority was found in the official texts consulted. The Court Guide and Factsheet and the Convention text agree word for word on the Article 15(2) clause and on the Article 2 exception.

CONCLUSIONS (for the results fields)

Ask 1 (verdict): No. A Contracting State invoking Article 15 during a war may not derogate from Article 3.

Ask 2 (value / identifier): The narrow Article 2 exception stated in Article 15(2) is: deaths resulting from lawful acts of war.

End of memorandum. This draft is for attorney review and is not legal advice.
cautions: Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 5 on echr.coe.int/documents/604084/839313/convention_eng.pdf/b404eea8-cbb3-177e-db52-6e6759f3bfc8?version=1.1&t=1675077491200&download=true and 15 on prd-echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/fs_derogation_eng. The first reads: "No derogation from this Article shall be made under Article15 of the Convention."

answer:

MEMORANDUM

To: Cross-border contracts team
From: Legal Researcher
Re: Which UNCITRAL text to retrieve for a model arbitration framework covering (i) the arbitration agreement, (ii) tribunal composition and jurisdiction, (iii) court intervention, and (iv) recognition and enforcement of the award
Jurisdiction: International UNCITRAL model-law framework. The Model Law is a legislative template for States to enact; it is not a treaty and has no force of its own. It governs a particular arbitration only to the extent that the law of the seat (or another enacting State whose law is applicable) adopts it. No seat or enacting State was specified in the request, so no national arbitration statute is applied in this memorandum. Cross-border recognition and enforcement of awards is additionally governed, in Contracting States, by the 1958 New York Convention; the Convention text was not retrieved in this iteration and is flagged below as a companion instrument, not as law applied here.

1. ANSWER (ask 2)

Retrieve the UNCITRAL Model Law on International Commercial Arbitration (1985), with amendments as adopted in 2006.

Retrieve the 2006 amended version, not the original 1985 text. UNCITRAL's official page for the instrument states: 'Amendments to articles 1 (2), 7, and 35 (2), a new chapter IV A to replace article 17 and a new article 2 A were adopted by UNCITRAL on 7 July 2006. ... As of 2006, the standard version of the Model Law is the amended version. The original 1985 text is also reproduced in view of the many national enactments based on this original version.' [Source: https://uncitral.un.org/en/texts/arbitration/modellaw/commercial_arbitration, fetched 2026-11-23T00:04:14Z, sha256 2b767ee0758e]

2. WHY THIS INSTRUMENT SATISFIES THE CONSTRAINT (ask 1)

The four headings named in the request match, nearly verbatim, the Model Law's official scope statement: 'It covers all stages of the arbitral process from the arbitration agreement, the composition and jurisdiction of the arbitral tribunal and the extent of court intervention through to the recognition and enforcement of the arbitral award.' [Source: https://uncitral.un.org/en/texts/arbitration/modellaw/commercial_arbitration, fetched 2026-11-23T00:04:14Z, sha256 2b767ee0758e]

This is a legislative model — a statute for States to enact — not a one-paragraph contract clause and not a set of procedural rules for conducting a hearing. The four headings are structural headings of a national arbitration statute. A short model clause of the kind institutions publish for insertion into commercial contracts would not contain provisions on the extent of court intervention, competence of the tribunal to rule on its own jurisdiction, setting aside, or grounds for refusing enforcement.

Heading-by-heading mapping, using only the fetched primary texts:

(a) Arbitration agreement — Chapter II.
- Article 7 (definition and form). The 2006 revision of Article 7 was intended 'to modernise the form required of an arbitration agreement to better conform with international contract practices.' [Source: https://uncitral.un.org/en/texts/arbitration/modellaw/commercial_arbitration, fetched 2026-11-23T00:04:14Z, sha256 2b767ee0758e]. The 2006 text presents Article 7 as 'Option I ... (As adopted by the Commission at its thirty-ninth session, in 2006)': an arbitration agreement is an agreement to submit to arbitration disputes which have arisen or may arise in respect of a defined legal relationship, whether contractual or not, and may be a clause in a contract or a separate agreement. [Source: https://uncitral.un.org/sites/uncitral.un.org/files/media-documents/uncitral/en/07-86998_ebook.pdf, fetched 2026-11-23T00:04:17Z, sha256 4b2c5a4f7340]
- Article 8 (arbitration agreement and substantive claim before court). A court before which an action is brought in a matter which is the subject of an arbitration agreement shall, if a party so requests not later than when submitting his first statement on the substance of the dispute, refer the parties to arbitration unless it finds that the agreement is null and void, inoperative or incapable of being performed. [Source: https://uncitral.un.org/sites/uncitral.un.org/files/media-documents/uncitral/en/07-86998_ebook.pdf, fetched 2026-11-23T00:04:17Z, sha256 4b2c5a4f7340]

MEMORANDUM

To: Reviewing Attorney
From: Legal Researcher
Re: Original applicability of the Federal Rules of Evidence to further procedure in an action pending on the effective date; treatment where application would not be feasible or would work injustice
Jurisdiction: United States federal courts
Status: Draft for attorney review. Not legal advice. Not an application to any specific pending case.

I. QUESTION PRESENTED

An action was already pending when the Federal Rules of Evidence took effect. Under the rules' original applicability provisions: (a) do the rules govern further procedure in that action; and (b) what happens to the extent that applying them would not be feasible or would work injustice?

II. SHORT ANSWER

Yes. The original effective-date and application provision provides that the rules "also apply to further procedure in actions, cases, and proceedings then pending." They do so by their own terms; no new filing or post-effective-date pleading is required. The same provision then states the prescribed consequence of infeasibility or injustice: "except to the extent that application of the rules would not be feasible, or would work injustice, in which event former evidentiary principles apply." The exception is partial ("to the extent"), not an all-or-nothing election, and it substitutes former evidentiary principles for the new rules only in the respect and to the extent the exception is found to apply. It does not reopen, unwind, or invalidate procedure already completed before July 1, 1975.

III. CONTROLLING PRIMARY TEXT (QUOTED IN FULL)

The governing source is the enactment and effective-date section of the Federal Rules of Evidence Act, not current Rule 1101:

Pub. L. No. 93-595, § 1, Jan. 2, 1975, 88 Stat. 1926 (Effective Date and Application of Rules), provided:

"That the following rules shall take effect on the one hundred and eightieth day [July 1, 1975] beginning after the date of the enactment of this Act [Jan. 2, 1975]. These rules apply to actions, cases, and proceedings brought after the rules take effect. These rules also apply to further procedure in actions, cases, and proceedings then pending, except to the extent that application of the rules would not be feasible, or would work injustice, in which event former evidentiary principles apply."

That text is confirmed in the 2021 U.S. Code compilation of Title 28, Appendix — Rules of Evidence (Historical Note to the Rules), and in the LII/Wex publication of the Federal Rules of Evidence under "Effective Date and Application of Rules."

The historical note to the same compilation records that the Rules were adopted by order of the Supreme Court on November 20, 1972, transmitted to Congress on February 5, 1973, that Pub. L. 93-12, March 30, 1973, 87 Stat. 9, provided the proposed rules "shall have no force or effect except to the extent, and with such amendments, as they may be expressly approved by Act of Congress," and that Pub. L. 93-595 enacted the Rules, with congressional amendments, to take effect July 1, 1975. The pending-action clause is therefore an Act of Congress, not a Supreme Court promulgation standing alone.

Original Article XI / Rule 1101 (Applicability of Rules), as in force before the 2011 restyling, addressed to which courts and to which categories of proceedings the Rules applied (United States district courts, district courts of Guam, the Virgin Islands, and the Northern Mariana Islands, courts of appeals, the Claims Court / Court of Federal Claims, bankruptcy judges and magistrate judges; civil actions including admiralty and maritime, criminal cases and proceedings, contempt proceedings except those in which the court may act summarily, and cases under title 11; privilege rules at all stages; enumerated exceptions). Original Rule 1101 did not itself contain the pending-action transition sentence or the infeasibility/injustice clause. Those provisions lived in section 1 of the 1975 Act, quoted above.

IV. ANALYSIS

A. Ask 2 — Verdict: the rules govern further procedure in a then-pending action

The statutory text answers this affirmatively in two steps. First, the default for new matters: the rules "apply to actions, cases, and proceedings brought after the rules take effect." Second, the express pending-action clause: they "also apply to further procedure in actions, cases, and proceedings then pending." The word "also" makes pending actions a covered category, not an omission to be filled by inference. The operative date is the effective date, July 1, 1975 (the one hundred eightieth day after January 2, 1975).

"Further procedure" means proceedings occurring on or after the effective date. It does not mean that completed pre-effective-date rulings, trial events, or evidentiary determinations are reopened, re-adjudicated, or invalidated. Nothing in the quoted text authorizes retroactive disturbance of finished procedure; it reaches only further procedure.

The clause is not limited to civil actions. It uses "actions, cases, and proceedings then pending," which on its face includes criminal prosecutions and other proceedings within Rule 1101's then-existing scope. No civil/criminal distinction is drawn in the transition sentence itself.

The rules therefore govern further procedure in the pending action by the provision's own terms. The verdict is yes.

B. Ask 3 — Value: what happens where application would not be feasible or would work injustice

The same sentence supplies the exception and its consequence:

- Trigger: application of the rules "would not be feasible, or would work injustice."
- Scope: "to the extent that" — the exception is measured by the respect in which infeasibility or injustice is shown, not by a binary choice between the entire old regime and the entire new code.
- Consequence: "in which event former evidentiary principles apply."

The prescribed treatment is therefore substitution of the pre-Rules evidentiary principles for the new Rules, in the particular respect and to the particular extent that the exception is satisfied. Where the exception does not apply, the new Rules govern the further procedure. The exception is an express statutory carve-out; it is not a judicial equitable override of the Act.

The text does not define "not feasible" or "work injustice," does not identify who decides (though the later § 2074 analog places the judgment in "the opinion of the court in which such proceedings are pending"), and does not prescribe a burden of proof or a showing standard. Those construction questions are not resolved by the primary statutory text retrieved for this memorandum.

C. The exception is not in current Rule 1101

Current (restyled, effective December 1, 2011) Rule 1101 states to whom and in what cases the Rules apply. It does not contain the 1975 pending-action transition language or the infeasibility/injustice clause. That omission is expected: the 1975 transition was a one-time statutory effective-date rule, not a standing rule of applicability. For later-amended rules, the standing analog is 28 U.S.C. § 2074 (added Pub. L. 100-702, title IV, § 401(a), November 19, 1988, 102 Stat. 4649, effective December 1, 1988), which provides that the Supreme Court "may fix the extent such rule shall apply to proceedings then pending, except that the Supreme Court shall not require the application of such rule to further proceedings then pending to the extent that, in the opinion of the court in which such proceedings are pending, the application of such rule in such proceedings would not be feasible or would work injustice, in which event the former rule applies." Section 2074 governs subsequent amendments prescribed under § 2072; it is not the source of the original 1975 transition, though it preserves the same infeasibility/injustice concept and attributes the judgment to the court in which the proceedings are pending.

V. WHAT THE TEXT DOES NOT ESTABLISH (THIN AUTHORITY)

The following points are not established by the primary sources retrieved, and this draft does not fill them from outside authority:

1. Judicial construction of "not feasible" and of "work injustice" — including what showing a party must make, whether the burden is on the party resisting the Rules, and whether injustice requires prejudice from reliance on pre-Rules practice — is not developed in any court decision among the retrieved primary sources. The standard is discretionary in character on the face of the statute; how courts have articulated it would require a separate pull of decided cases, which has not been done here.

2. Whether any constitutional or independent statutory limit independently restricts application of the Rules to further procedure in a then-pending criminal case is not addressed by the retrieved sources. The transition text itself contains no criminal-specific carve-out.

3. The retrieved Conference report fragment ("The Conference adopts the House provision") confirms congressional-branch adoption of a House provision but does not, standing alone, supply the legislative intent behind the infeasibility/injustice clause beyond the enacted words.

A reviewing attorney who needs the judicial gloss on the exception should commission that case research; it is not honestly supplied from the materials in hand.

VI. APPLICATION FRAME (for attorney use on a concrete matter)

If this question is being applied to a real file:

1. Confirm the forum is a United States federal court within the scope of the Rules (original Rule 1101 / current Rule 1101(a)–(b)).
2. Confirm the relevant proceeding step occurs on or after July 1, 1975. If the step was completed before that date, the pending-action clause does not reach it.
3. Default: the Rules govern the further procedure.
4. Exception: a party invoking the carve-out must identify the specific respect in which application would not be feasible or would work injustice. If that showing is accepted, former evidentiary principles apply only to that extent. The exception is not a free election to live entirely under pre-1975 evidence law.
5. Do not cite current Rule 1101 for the pending-action transition or the infeasibility/injustice clause; cite Pub. L. 93-595, § 1, 88 Stat. 1926. For post-1988 amendments, cite 28 U.S.C. § 2074 instead.

VII. CONCLUSIONS STATED

Ask 2 (verdict): Yes. Under the original applicability provisions, the Federal Rules of Evidence govern further procedure in an action, case, or proceeding that was pending when the Rules took effect on July 1, 1975.

Ask 3 (value): Former evidentiary principles apply — to the extent that application of the Rules would not be feasible or would work injustice. That is the statutory consequence. Outside that extent, the Rules apply.

PRIMARY SOURCES CITED IN FULL

1. Act of Jan. 2, 1975, Pub. L. No. 93-595, § 1, 88 Stat. 1926 (Federal Rules of Evidence Act; effective date and application provision quoted in full in Section III).
2. Act of Mar. 30, 1973, Pub. L. No. 93-12, 87 Stat. 9 (withholding force from the proposed rules except as expressly approved by Act of Congress).
3. 28 U.S.C. app. Fed. R. Evid. (2021 compilation), Historical Note, at https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2021-title28/pdf/USCODE-2021-title28-app-federalru-dup2.pdf.
4. Federal Rules of Evidence, Effective Date and Application of Rules, Legal Information Institute, https://www.law.cornell.edu/rules/fre.
5. Fed. R. Evid. 1101 (current, restyled eff. Dec. 1, 2011), United States Courts, https://www.uscourts.gov/file/rules-evidence.
6. 28 U.S.C. § 2074 (added Pub. L. No. 100-702, title IV, § 401(a), Nov. 19, 1988, 102 Stat. 4649, eff. Dec. 1, 1988), quoted in the United States Courts publications of the Rules of Evidence.
7. Fed. R. Evid. 1101 (pre-restyling text), United States Courts, https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/federal_rules/FREP12.1.08.pdf.
